question: What are the 3 main ready-to-cook carcass grading factors?
answer: Exposed flesh, missing parts, and disjointed/broken bones.

question: How should you determine the final carcass grade with multiple defects?
answer: Always score based on the lowest-grade defect found.

question: Define what counts as 'exposed flesh' in carcass grading.
answer: Cuts, tears, or trims showing meat/flesh because the skin is missing or damaged.

question: What is the maximum cut/tear allowed on the BREAST of a 2-6 lb Grade A carcass?
answer: Less than 1/4 inch total with no missing skin.

question: For a Grade B 2-6 lb carcass, what is the flesh exposure limit on the entire BREAST?
answer: Up to 1/3 of the flesh can be exposed on the entire breast.

question: How much exposed flesh determines a Grade C carcass on the breast?
answer: More than 1/3 of the flesh exposed on the entire breast.

question: What is the Grade A limit for cuts on WINGS and BACK (2-6 lb carcass)?
answer: Up to 1 1/2 inches for Grade A.

question: Are cuts/tears on a carcass additive across different parts?
answer: No. Cuts are cumulative only within one part, not across multiple parts.

question: When do deep cuts (>1/8 inch) change the carcass grade beyond exposed flesh limits?
answer: Deep cuts without meat removal don't change grade beyond exposed flesh designation.

question: What is the maximum trim size that does NOT affect carcass grade?
answer: Trims not exceeding 1/8 inch thickness (nickel) and 0.75 inch diameter (quarter).

question: What happens when meat is trimmed beyond the Grade A limits from breast or legs?
answer: Carcass is marked NO GRADE (loss of marketable product).

question: Are processing cuts near vent/breast less than 1 inch acceptable?
answer: Yes, processing cuts less than 1 inch beyond opening are acceptable.

question: Which parts are considered in missing parts grading?
answer: Wings, tail, and back. Missing parts elsewhere result in NO GRADE.

question: What wing removal is allowed for Grade A?
answer: One or both wing TIPS can be removed.

question: What wing removal is allowed for Grade B?
answer: One or both wings removed to the second joint.

question: What wing removal is allowed for Grade C?
answer: One or both whole wings cut cleanly at body juncture without breast meat removal.

question: What results in NO GRADE regarding wing removal?
answer: Breast meat trimmed with removal of whole wing.

question: How is the tail removed for a Grade A carcass?
answer: Removed at its base.

question: How is the back area removed for a Grade B carcass?
answer: Back area not wider than tail base and only halfway to hip joint.

question: How is the back area removed for a Grade C carcass?
answer: Back area not wider than tail base but extends beyond hip joints.

question: What results in NO GRADE for back/tail removal?
answer: Back trimmed wider than tail base resulting in meat loss.

question: Define a disjointed bone.
answer: Ball end of joint is out of socket; part is whole, not broken.

question: What is the difference between protruding and non-protruding broken bones?
answer: Non-protruding: bone broken but doesn't come through skin. Protruding: bone ruptures through skin.

question: How many disjointed/broken bones are allowed on a Grade A?
answer: One disjointed bone; NO broken bones allowed.

question: What combinations are allowed on a Grade B carcass?
answer: Two disjointed bones OR one disjointed and one non-protruding broken bone.

question: What bone defects make a carcass Grade C?
answer: More than two disjointed or non-protruding broken bones, or ANY protruding broken bones.

question: Which 10 parts are used in 4-H RTC parts grading?
answer: Breast quarter, breast quarter without wing, leg quarter, whole leg, thigh, thigh with back, drumstick, whole wing, wing drumette, wing flat.

question: For broiler parts (2-6 lb), what skin cut allows Grade A exposed flesh?
answer: A cut up to 1/4 inch.

question: How much skin must remain attached on a Grade A part?
answer: At least 75 percent of normal skin cover must remain attached.

question: How much exposed flesh is allowed for Grade B parts?
answer: Up to 1/3 of the flesh on the entire part.

question: Which parts can have disjointed bones in parts grading?
answer: Thighs with back, whole legs, leg quarters, and whole wings.

question: Can Grade A leg quarters have disjointed bones?
answer: Yes, femur may be disjointed from hip socket in Grade A.

question: What grade results from any disjointed wing?
answer: Any disjointed wing automatically results in Grade B.

question: What happens with broken or cut bones in parts grading?
answer: Any broken or cut bone automatically results in Grade C.

question: List the 5 judging criteria for breaded boneless poultry products.
answer: Coating defect, consistency of shape/size, cluster/aggregate, completeness of product, foreign material.

question: What continuous void size is a defect on PATTIES?
answer: Continuous void greater than 1/2 inch.

question: What continuous void size is a defect on NUGGETS/TENDERS?
answer: Continuous void greater than 1/4 inch.

question: Are coating voids on a single product additive?
answer: No, voids on one product are not added together.

question: What color breading is expected?
answer: A golden-brown color.

question: When is uneven color a defect in a group of 3 products?
answer: When one product is noticeably darker/lighter than the other two.

question: For single products, when is color a defect?
answer: When not uniform across item; has dark, burnt, or contrasting colored areas.

question: When is shape/size consistency a defect?
answer: Substantial differences in shape/size affecting consumer preferences/cook times.

question: What defines a cluster defect?
answer: Two or more pieces appear fused together with breading.

question: If products are just touching, is it a cluster defect?
answer: No, they must appear fused together with breading.

question: Define incomplete break in breaded products.
answer: Product has a break or tear in meat that is clearly visible.

question: Define complete break in breaded products.
answer: Product is broken apart and displayed as two pieces or part of a piece.

question: What are examples of foreign materials?
answer: Feathers, plastic, metal, rubber, glass, wood, or any non-food objects.

question: When one defect causes other defects, how do you score?
answer: Record main defect only; don't record secondary defects caused by primary one.

question: Is egg quality related to egg size or shell color?
answer: No, egg quality is independent of size and shell color.

question: What grades are used for contest egg exterior grading?
answer: A, B, Dirty, or Loss.

question: Can Grade A eggs show stains or marks?
answer: Yes, small specks, stains, or cage marks that don't detract from appearance.

question: Define cage marks.
answer: Marks or translucent lines from rusty/dirty cage wires or roll-out trays.

question: For Grade B with ONE stain (localized), what is the maximum stain size?
answer: Less than 1/32 of entire shell.

question: For Grade B with MULTIPLE stains (scattered), what is maximum total stain?
answer: Less than 1/16 of entire shell.

question: What classification are prominent stains?
answer: Dirty eggs.

question: What is adhering material vs small specks?
answer: Adhering material = 3-D objects like feathers. Small specks = dust/lint (ignored).

question: What egg shapes are Grade A?
answer: A considerable range of approximately normal shape (not spherical/round or too long).

question: When is an egg Grade B for shape?
answer: When spherical/round, too long for carton, clearly misshapen, or has flat areas.

question: What is the maximum size of calcium deposits for Grade A?
answer: Less than 1/8 inch diameter (multiple deposits OK if each <1/8 inch).

question: When are calcium deposits a Grade B defect?
answer: When any deposit is larger than 1/8 inch in diameter.

question: What shell roughness is acceptable for Grade A?
answer: Slight rough areas that don't materially affect shape or shell strength.

question: When is rough shell texture a Grade B defect?
answer: Extremely rough areas that may be faulty in soundness or strength.

question: When are shell ridges a Grade B defect?
answer: When they are large and result in weakened shells.

question: What is required for Grade A shell thickness?
answer: Thick shells with NO thin spots; withstand reasonable handling.

question: Define a window on eggshell.
answer: Small three-dimensional thin spot (distinct from cage marks).

question: What is a body check?
answer: Shell looks cracked but is intact; crack and then partial calcification during formation.

question: What grade is a body check egg?
answer: Grade B (shell intact but weak).

question: What is a check egg?
answer: Cracked shell but intact membrane; contents don't leak = Loss grade.

question: What is a leaker egg?
answer: Cracked shell where contents exude or are free to exude = Loss grade.

question: How should you hold an egg for candling?
answer: Small end between thumb/first two fingers; large end to light in slanting position.

question: What causes yolk movement to increase in older eggs?
answer: Albumen thins as egg ages; yolk moves more freely and approaches shell.

question: What does minimal yolk movement indicate?
answer: Fresh egg with firm, thick white; yolk surrounded by dense albumen layer.

question: What size blood/meat spots are Grade B?
answer: Small spots totaling less than 1/8 inch diameter.

question: What size blood/meat spots are Loss grade?
answer: Large spots greater than 1/8 inch diameter.

question: Define chalaza and how to distinguish from blood spot.
answer: Mucin fibers holding yolk centered; has bright refracted light unlike blood spots.

question: What air cell depth is Grade AA?
answer: 1/8 inch deep or less.

question: What air cell depth is Grade A?
answer: Greater than 1/8 inch but less than 3/16 inch.

question: What air cell depth is Grade B?
answer: More than 3/16 inch.

question: Why does air cell size increase as egg ages?
answer: Evaporation occurs, causing air cell to expand.

question: Describe Grade AA broken-out egg appearance.
answer: Thick albumen maintains egg shape; yolk sits high off plate.

question: Describe Grade A broken-out egg appearance.
answer: Albumen losing egg shape, rounding edges, sits lower; can't see under yolk.

question: Describe Grade B broken-out egg appearance.
answer: Yolk is flattened; thick albumen is mostly gone.

question: When grading broken-out eggs, which measurement is most important?
answer: Height of thick albumen (side view).

question: Should you compare eggs when grading broken-out quality?
answer: No, evaluate each egg on its own merit to avoid setting incorrect standards.

question: Should marination injection marks affect grading?
answer: No, ignore them; officials announce their presence.

question: Should off-color or dried-out areas affect carcass grade?
answer: No, do not grade based on off-color, bruised, or discolored dried areas.

question: Are feathers/pin-feathers considered in carcass grading?
answer: No, feathers/pin-feathers are NOT a quality factor.

question: Can you touch/handle carcasses during judging?
answer: No, but you can turn shackle to see all parts.

question: What weight categories are used in 4-H contest carcass grading?
answer: Only first two: broilers (2-6 lb) and heavy broilers.

question: Can any weight category be used for RTC parts grading?
answer: Yes, broiler, heavy broiler, and turkey parts can be used.

question: Can cracked/dirty eggs be used in contests?
answer: No, they are removed as Loss eggs.

question: Can excessively speckled brown eggs be used?
answer: No, they should not be used in contests.

question: Can handlers touch eggs during exterior grading?
answer: No, eggs are placed sideways on cartons; assume unseen side is clean.

question: How many weight classes are considered for determining defects?
answer: Two weight classes used for cut/tear sizing (broiler vs. heavy broiler).

question: How should contestants approach judging whole carcasses?
answer: Learn by looking at one part at a time; carcass has 6 parts: 2 wings, 2 legs, breast, back.

question: When you are judging breaded products, what should you evaluate?
answer: Only fully visible portions since contestants cannot handle products.

question: What grades are shown in this image based on breast cuts and tears?
answer: Grade A (less than 1/4 inch exposed), Grade B (up to 1/3 flesh exposed), and Grade C (more than 1/3 flesh exposed).

question: What grade are these carcasses with deep cuts (deeper than 1/8 inch)?
answer: Grade B - cuts deeper than 1/8 inch without meat removal do not change the grade beyond what is designated for exposed flesh.

question: What grades are shown based on meat trim in this image?
answer: Trims that exceed 1/8 inch thick or 0.75 inches diameter on breast/legs result in NO GRADE due to altered meat yield.

question: What grades are shown based on back and wing cuts?
answer: Grade A (cut up to 1Â½ inches), Grade B (up to 1/3 flesh exposed), Grade C (more than 1/3 flesh exposed).

question: What grade is this carcass with a processing cut at the neck and keel tip?
answer: Grade A - processing cuts less than 1 inch beyond the opening are acceptable. (Ignore marination injection marks.)

question: What grade is this carcass with processing cuts at neck and keel tip?
answer: Grade B - processing cuts larger than 1 inch downgrade to Grade B.

question: What grades are shown based on missing wings?
answer: Grade A (wing tips removed), Grade B (wing to second joint), Grade C (whole wing removed cleanly), NO GRADE (breast meat removed with wing).

question: What anatomical references are shown for missing backs?
answer: Tail base, hip joints, and width measurements used to determine grade for missing back portions.

question: What grades are shown based on missing tail and back?
answer: Grade A (tail removed at base), Grade B (back not wider than tail base to halfway to hip), Grade C (beyond hip joints), NO GRADE (wider than tail base).

question: What grade are these carcasses with one disjointed bone?
answer: Grade A - can have one disjointed bone (wing or leg shown). Compare how disjointed parts hang differently.

question: What grade are these carcasses with two disjoints?
answer: Grade B - can have two disjointed bones (shown: two wings, or one wing plus one leg).

question: What grade are these carcasses with broken non-protruding bones?
answer: Grade B - can have one broken non-protruding bone (shown: broken wing and broken drumstick).

question: What grade are these carcasses with protruding broken bones?
answer: Grade C - any protruding broken bone makes the carcass Grade C (shown: broken wing and broken drumstick).

question: How are carcasses displayed for judging?
answer: Hung from shackles either by both legs or one leg. Cannot be touched during judging; tilt shackle to check for broken bones.

question: What do clean, normal-shaped Grade A eggs look like?
answer: Clean appearance with regular oval shape. Both white and brown eggs shown meeting Grade A cleanliness standards.

question: What are cage marks and how do they affect grading?
answer: Marks/translucent lines from cage wires. Small marks not detracting from appearance = Grade A; darker marks detracting = Grade B; large 3D marks = dirty.

question: What do the 1/16 and 1/32 shell area references look like?
answer: Visual reference showing relative shell areas: Grade B allows localized stain <1/32 or scattered stains <1/16 of entire shell.

question: What grades result from different stain patterns?
answer: Shows localized vs scattered stains. Grade B: single stain <1/32 or multiple <1/16 total. Larger stains = dirty.

question: What types of adhering material are shown?
answer: Manure, feather, and egg yolk. Adhering material (3-dimensional) larger than a speck = dirty egg.

question: What shape defects result in Grade B?
answer: Eggs that are too round (spherical) or too long to fit in carton. Also misshapen or with definite flat areas.

question: How do calcium deposits affect egg grading?
answer: Grade A: each deposit <1/8 inch (any number allowed). Grade B: any deposit â‰¥1/8 inch diameter.

question: What grade are eggs with extreme shell roughness?
answer: Grade B - extreme rough areas that may be faulty in soundness or strength. (Grade A may have slight rough areas.)

question: What grade are eggs with large shell ridges?
answer: Grade B - large ridges result in weakened shells.

question: What grade are eggs with thin spots or 'windows'?
answer: Grade B - thin shells or thin spots (windows must be 3-dimensional). Grade A must have thick shells with no thin spots.

question: What is a body check and what grade is it?
answer: Grade B - shell looks cracked but is intact. Occurs during shell formation when cracked then partially calcified before laying. Shell is weak when candled.

question: What grade is a cracked egg?
answer: Loss - broken shell or crack in shell (even if membranes intact and contents don't leak). Also called 'checked' egg.

question: What defect is shown in this chicken patty?
answer: COATING DEFECT - continuous breading void greater than Â½ inch in diameter (patties must have voids >Â½ inch to be defect).

question: Is this chicken patty defective?
answer: No defect - coating void is less than Â½ inch. Patties need continuous void >Â½ inch to be coating defect.

question: Is this chicken patty with two coating voids defective?
answer: No defect - each void is less than Â½ inch. Voids on a single product are NOT added together.

question: What defect is shown in this chicken patty?
answer: COATING DEFECT - uneven color with burnt breading. Color should be uniform across product without dark burnt areas or contrasting colors.

question: What defect is shown between these two patties?

question: What defect is shown with these overlapping patties?
answer: CLUSTER/AGGREGATE OF PRODUCTS - two patties fused together with breading (not just touching). May not cook properly.

question: What defect is shown in this chicken patty?
answer: COMPLETENESS OF PRODUCT - incomplete break (break/tear in meat clearly visible but not separated).

question: What defect is shown in this broken chicken patty?
answer: COMPLETENESS OF PRODUCT - complete break (product broken apart and displayed in two pieces or as partial piece).

question: What defect is shown in these chicken patties?
answer: FOREIGN MATERIAL - protruding piece of non-food object (feathers, plastic, metal, rubber, glass, wood).

question: What multiple defects are shown in these patties?
answer: Left: COMPLETENESS OF PRODUCT + COATING DEFECT. Right: COMPLETENESS + COATING + FOREIGN MATERIAL (three defects).

question: What defects are present in this group of patties?
answer: COATING DEFECT on 1st and 2nd (burnt/missing coating), COMPLETENESS on 3rd (break), CONSISTENCY OF SHAPE/SIZE (difference between patties).

question: What is the proper technique for holding an egg for candling?
answer: Hold small end between thumb and first two fingers. Place large end up to candling light in slanting position. Turn wrist back and forth to twirl contents.

question: How do you use the USDA air cell gauge for grading?
answer: Hold gauge to candled egg. Grade AA: â‰¤1/8 inch, Grade A: >1/8 to <3/16 inch, Grade B: â‰¥3/16 inch air cell depth.

question: What grades do these air cell depths represent?
answer: 1) Grade AA (<1/8"), 2) Grade A (>1/8"), 3) Same Grade A egg (<3/16"), 4) Grade B (>3/16").

question: What type of spot is shown in this broken-out egg?
answer: Blood spot on the yolk. If blood/meat spots total <1/8 inch diameter = Grade B; if â‰¥1/8 inch = Loss.

question: What type of spot is shown in this broken-out egg?
answer: Meat spot in the albumen. If blood/meat spots total <1/8 inch diameter = Grade B; if â‰¥1/8 inch = Loss.

question: What is shown in the albumen of this broken-out egg?
answer: Chalaza (NOT a meat spot). Chalazae are mucin fiber strands holding yolk in center - distinguished by bright refracted light area with darker shadow.

question: What grade is this broken-out egg?
answer: Grade AA - thick albumen in egg shape, yolk sits high off plate. Evaluate height of thick albumen (side view), not just diameter.

question: What grade is this broken-out egg?
answer: Grade A - albumen losing egg shape, sits lower on plate. Edges of thick albumen have rounding. Cannot see under the yolk.

question: What grade is this broken-out egg?
answer: Grade B - yolk is flattened, thick albumen is almost all gone. Evaluate each egg on its own merit, don't compare with others.

question: What are the USDA standards for broken-out egg grades?
answer: Visual chart showing Grade AA (high, firm albumen), Grade A (reasonably firm), Grade B (weak, watery albumen with flat yolk).

question: What are the labeled parts of an egg shown?
answer: Shell, air cell, membranes, chalazae (holding yolk in center), albumen (egg white), yolk, germinal disc.
